section_title: What consequence follows the messenger’s disobedience?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 20 While they were sitting at the table, the word of the LORD came to the prophet who had brought him back, 21 and the prophet cried out to the man of God who had come from Judah, “This is what the LORD says: ‘Because you have defied the word of the LORD and have not kept the commandment that the LORD your God gave you, 22 but you went back and ate bread and drank water in the place where He told you not to do so, your body shall never reach the tomb of your fathers.’”

23 And after the man of God had finished eating and drinking, the old prophet who had brought him back saddled the donkey for him. 24 As he went on his way, a lion met him on the road and killed him, and his body was left lying in the road, with the donkey and the lion standing beside it. 25 And there were men passing by who saw the body lying in the road with the lion standing beside it, and they went and reported this in the city where the old prophet lived.

context_lines: At the table, a genuine word from the LORD comes to the prophet who brought the man back. He announces that the man from Judah has disobeyed God’s command and will not be buried in his ancestors’ tomb.
After the meal, the man departs on a donkey. A lion meets him on the road and kills him. Passing travelers see his body with the lion and donkey standing nearby, and report it in the city.
The account makes the announced consequence part of the same story as the deception. The messenger who delivered God’s warning also had to heed the command given to him.
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-kings/) emphasizes the seriousness of disregarding a direct command, rather than judging the act only by how ordinary a meal may seem. [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_kings/13.htm) also sees a warning that a person’s office or earlier service does not make disobedience harmless.

Both writers address the difficult question of why the deceiver is not shown receiving the same immediate punishment. They look beyond present events to God’s final judgment. The narrative does not supply the old prophet’s whole future, and its silence should not be turned into approval of his lie.
